issues.body:
## [RL] Comprehensive Feature Checklist for RL Parity

This issue tracks a **comprehensive, framework-neutral feature checklist** for the RL stack the OpenThoughts/Marin team currently relies on (MarinSkyRL), intended as a parity yardstick for any RL framework we build on or migrate to.

It was assembled from an **evidence-based inventory** of:
- every present and deprecated SkyRL config under `OpenThoughts-Agent/hpc/skyrl_yaml/` (jupiter / ALCC / leonardo / ZIH / deprecated),
- the Leonardo one-off grids/launch scripts (`gsm8k_grid_leonardo`, `opd_grid_leonardo` — efficiency + on-policy-distillation sweeps),
- the MarinSkyRL codebase (`skyrl-train`, `skyrl-gym`, `skyrl-agent`, `skyrl-tx`),
- and the MoE / router-replay design corpus.

The full checklist is posted **as a comment below**, organized by area (algorithms, dense + MoE architectures, sync/async, inference, efficiency/scaling, agentic incl. the terminal-bench entrypoint, non-agentic RLVR, on-policy distillation, optimizers, reward & regularization, hooks/observability, infra/ops). Each item is annotated with its current state in our stack:

- ✅ have-and-rely-on
- ⚠️ partial / exercised but not hardened / experimental
- ❌ want-but-missing

**Headline gaps** (honestly flagged): MoE + Expert Parallelism + grouped-GEMM + DeepEP-at-scale + **router replay (R3)** are the least-mature surface — ported and validated to a single 80B (Qwen3-Next-A3B) capstone training step, but not production-hardened for multi-step stability, with the Megatron-path hybrid arch and DeepEP-at-scale still missing.

cc @rjpower — flagging for your visibility / input on prioritization.

---
*Source inventory + wishlist live in `notes/RL/wishlist/` (`MARINSKYRL_FEATURE_INVENTORY.md`, `RL_FRAMEWORK_WISHLIST.md`).*

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖 **Comprehensive RL Parity feature checklist** (vetted for duplicates/gaps).

# RL Framework Parity Wish List

A framework-neutral checklist of everything an RL framework would need to reach parity with
(and extend) the RL stack the OpenThoughts/Marin team currently relies on. Built from a
grepped, evidence-based inventory of all our SkyRL configs (current + deprecated), Leonardo
grid/launch scripts, the MarinSkyRL codebase, and the MoE/router-replay design corpus.

**Legend** — current state in *our present stack*:
✅ have-and-rely-on · ⚠️ partial / exercised but not hardened / experimental · ❌ want-but-missing

> This is a "what we want in an RL framework" parity list, not advocacy for any one framework.
> Items are checkboxes for tracking; the ✅/⚠️/❌ annotates where we are today.

---

## Core RL algorithms
- [ ] ✅ GRPO (group-relative advantage, std-normalization toggle)
- [ ] ✅ RLOO and **RLOO-N** (leave-one-out baseline that excludes masked samples; min-group-size + zero-variance-group filtering) — our production default
- [ ] ✅ REINFORCE++ and GAE (with a critic/value head)
- [ ] ✅ Pluggable advantage-estimator + policy-loss **registries** (register custom variants without forking)
- [ ] ✅ PPO clip (`regular`) and asymmetric clip (low/high ε) with **dual-clip** (OpenHands-style, high≈0.28)
- [ ] ✅ **GSPO** (group sequence policy optimization, sequence-mean reduction)
- [ ] ⚠️ SAPO / CISPO / clip-cov / kl-cov policy losses (implemented; not yet exercised by us)
- [ ] ✅ `no_op` advantage + importance-sampling loss path (for distillation objectives)
- [ ] ❌ Critic-based PPO actually run at scale (we are value-free; GAE/critic exists but unused)

## Model architectures
### Dense
- [ ] ✅ Dense transformer RL (Qwen3-8B / 32B, Qwen2.5, Qwen3-1.7B) on FSDP2
- [ ] ✅ FSDP2 training backend (sharding, reshard-after-forward, CPU/param offload)
- [ ] ⚠️ DeepSpeed backend (implemented; not our production path)
- [ ] ⚠️ Megatron 5D-parallel backend (TP/PP/CP/EP/ETP) — implemented upstream, **never launched by us** (one untested design-artifact config)
- [ ] ✅ YaRN / rope-scaling for long context (131k); FP8 weights/sync
- [ ] ⚠️ LoRA RL (config surface present, unused)

### MoE — the big gap to harden
- [ ] ⚠️ MoE RL training at all (Mixtral-8x7B, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, GLM-4.6 teacher) — exercised, not hardened
- [ ] ⚠️ **Expert Parallelism (EP)** on a non-Megatron (FSDP2/DTensor) mesh — ported (Stages 4–7), torch-backend all-to-all validated, 80B capstone step reached
- [ ] ⚠️ **Grouped-GEMM** expert compute (vs eager per-expert Python loop)
- [ ] ❌ **DeepEP** fused dispatch/combine at scale (NVSHMEM; aarch64/cu13 wheel an open risk — torch-EP is the fallback floor)
- [ ] ⚠️ **Qwen3-Next hybrid arch** (GatedDeltaNet linear-attention + 512-expert top-10 + shared expert) end-to-end RL — capstone training step done, multi-step stability still being hardened
- [ ] ⚠️ Qwen3-MoE / standard-attention MoE families
- [ ] ❌ MoE on the Megatron path for our hybrid arch (AutoBridge support for GatedDeltaNet is an open unknown)
- [ ] ❌ MoE aux/load-balancing loss in the RL loss (deliberately *not* wired — reward grads should flow to high-reward experts; flag for future optional router-bias update)

### Router replay (R3) — a desired MoE-correctness feature
- [ ] ⚠️ **Rollout Routing Replay (R3, arXiv 2510.11370)**: replay the rollout's per-token expert selection in the training forward (force top-k; keep gating gradients from live logits) so π_old == π_train for the MoE
- [ ] ⚠️ routed_experts **capture rail**: inference engine emits `[gen_len, num_layers, top_k]` over the OpenAI `/v1` API → rollout harness `extra` → trainer batch, token-aligned through sample packing + hybrid (non-uniform MoE-layer) layouts
- [ ] ⚠️ Replay correctness under sample packing and under EP all-to-all permute (per-token index alignment)
- [ ] ⚠️ Gradient-checkpointing × router-replay recompute-safety
- [ ] ❌ R3 as a first-class, framework-native feature (today it's a port/patch everywhere — not in megatron.core)

## Sync / async training
- [ ] ✅ Synchronous colocated training (policy+gen on shared GPUs)
- [ ] ✅ **Fully-async** disaggregated generation/training pipeline with bounded staleness (`max_staleness_steps`)
- [ ] ✅ Tunable generation-worker pool sized to engine fleet (oversubscription without trainer starvation)
- [ ] ✅ **Off-policy correction — TIS** (Truncated Importance Sampling, ratio cap) for stale/divergent rollouts
- [ ] ✅ Weight-transfer/sync modes: NCCL broadcast, CUDA-IPC (threshold-batched), FP8 fused-weight sync into the engine
- [ ] ⚠️ **StaleClip** staleness-aware regularizer (LR damping on stale + reward-concentrated batches) — exercised in ablations
- [ ] ❌ Adaptive/automatic staleness↔throughput controller (today it's hand-tuned per cluster)

## Inference / generation
- [ ] ✅ vLLM backend, colocated **and** disaggregated; engines launched locally; HTTP `/v1` endpoint for external harnesses
- [ ] ⚠️ SGLang backend (implemented; unused by us)
- [ ] ✅ Inference sharding: TP, PP, EP, DP per engine; N independent engines
- [ ] ✅ vLLM **`mp` executor backend** (non-Ray) — required where Ray Compiled-DAG deadlocks (hybrid-arch routed_experts capture)
- [ ] ✅ Engine efficiency knobs: prefix caching, chunked prefill, cudagraph vs enforce-eager, gpu-memory-utilization, max_num_seqs / max_num_batched_tokens, kv-cache dtype, quantization (AWQ/marlin), custom chat templates
- [ ] ✅ **routed_experts emission over `/v1`** (our `mlfoundations/vllm` fork + HTTP serialization patch) for R3 capture
- [ ] ✅ Per-token rollout logprob capture from the engine (required for TIS)
- [ ] ✅ Interleaved-thinking chat template that preserves `<think>` blocks across turns
- [ ] ✅ Sampling control: temp/top_p/top_k/min_p/repetition_penalty, separate eval sampling, DAPO overlong filtering, zero-reward-on-non-stop

## Efficiency / scaling
- [ ] ✅ Sequence packing + micro-batching (separate forward/train micro sizes)
- [ ] ✅ Gradient checkpointing (reentrant + non-reentrant) and activation/CPU/param offload (e.g. GH200 coherent LPDDR)
- [ ] ✅ FSDP `reshard_after_forward` toggle; `fsdp_size` control
- [ ] ✅ CUDA graphs / `torch.compile` / prefix cache as tunable throughput axes
- [ ] ✅ Multinode topology: SLURM + Ray-on-container bring-up; explicit policy/ref/engine node placement
- [ ] ✅ Deterministic GPU placement to avoid policy/engine collision OOM on full clusters (strict-spread PG, per-GPU bundles, CVD masking)
- [ ] ✅ Grid-sweepable efficiency axes (tp, n_samples, train/micro batch, colocate on/off, reshard, gmu, cudagraph, engine count)
- [ ] ❌ Auto memory-profiled microbatch/recompute selection (today hand-sized per model+cluster)

## Agentic support
- [ ] ✅ Multi-turn env abstraction (turns, tools, conversation-vs-appended multi-turn formatting)
- [ ] ✅ **Terminal-bench entrypoint**: agentic RL where an external agent (terminus-2) runs in a sandbox and calls the training engine over `/v1`
- [ ] ✅ **Harbor-style external-rollout seam**: pluggable harness that owns the agent loop, sandbox, and verifier and returns reward + trajectory + token-fidelity (logprobs, routed_experts) through an `extra` channel
- [ ] ✅ Sandbox backends: Daytona (cloud), Beam; docker/modal referenced — selectable via `environment_type`
- [ ] ✅ Sandbox/snapshot pooling: hash-based auto-snapshot caching, per-job concurrency cap, connection-pool sharding
- [ ] ✅ **K-actor rollout fan-out**: shard orchestration across coordinator actors to break the single-event-loop GIL ceiling
- [ ] ✅ Agent error classification: mask / passthrough / zero / exclude-from-retry per exception type (timeouts, context-overflow, network, env-start)
- [ ] ✅ Built-in single-turn agentic envs: gsm8k, aime, lcb, search, searchcode, sql
- [ ] ✅ Tool/agent scaffolds (react, codeact) with cross-trainer integrations (verl, tinker, openai)
- [ ] ✅ Trajectory archiving + post-run trace upload to HF (SFT dataset export)

## Non-agentic support (single-turn RLVR)
- [ ] ✅ Single-turn RLVR entrypoint (no harness/sandbox/internet) on local parquet datasets
- [ ] ✅ Built-in verifiable envs (gsm8k / math) with dataset builders
- [ ] ✅ Verifier interface returning binary or fractional reward
- [ ] ✅ Offline operation (HF/W&B offline, pre-staged model+data, NCCL env tuning) for air-gapped HPC

## On-policy distillation (OPD)
- [ ] ✅ Teacher→student distillation: separate teacher inference engine (own placement group, no weight sync)
- [ ] ✅ Teacher top-K logprob scoring of student rollouts; per-token KL (forward/reverse/JSD) reward
- [ ] ✅ Quantized teacher support (AWQ/marlin, e.g. 357B MoE teacher serving a small student)
- [ ] ✅ Dedicated distillation trainer + loss path (`no_op` advantage, importance-sampling loss, KL-in-reward)
- [ ] ✅ Both agentic (harness-driven) and non-agentic (local-dataset) OPD entrypoints

## Optimizers
- [ ] ✅ AdamW (production), with adam_betas / weight_decay / max_grad_norm / warmup scheduler
- [ ] ✅ Any `torch.optim` class by name (NAdam, RAdam, Adamax, SGD, RMSprop, Adafactor)
- [ ] ✅ **Muon** (momentum + orthogonalization) — exercised
- [ ] ✅ SGD/NAdam/RAdam optimizer-specific kwargs (momentum, nesterov) via passthrough
- [ ] ✅ Per-optimizer LR scheduling (constant-with-warmup) and grad-norm clipping (static + adaptive)

## Reward & regularization
- [ ] ✅ KL penalty: as loss **or** in-reward; estimators **k1/k2/k3/abs**; fixed **and** adaptive KL controller (target/horizon)
- [ ] ✅ Entropy bonus (coefficient-tunable)
- [ ] ✅ Loss reduction modes: token-mean, sequence-mean, **seq-mean-token-sum-norm** (per-seq) and **-global** (global length-unbiased denominator)
- [ ] ✅ Shaped rewards: simple (`pass_ratio` = passed/total tests) and **composite** (verifier + thinking-length + format-quality + command-quality weighting) with auto-detected parser + fallback
- [ ] ✅ **PRM (process reward / mid-trial)**: teacher-hint injection (external LLM) and thrashing-detector early-termination (Jaccard repetition)
- [ ] ✅ Length / context-timeout masking via error classification + input-token budget guard
- [ ] ✅ Advantage normalization (by-std toggle, batch-level) and overlong/non-stop reward zeroing
- [ ] ✅ Static grad-norm clipping (`max_grad_norm`)
- [ ] ⚠️ **ZClip** adaptive EMA grad-norm spike clipping (exercised in ablations; StaleClip variant under *Sync/async*)
- [ ] ⚠️ Dynamic sampling (filter/replace low-variance groups) — implemented, unused

## Hooks / callbacks / observability
- [ ] ✅ Trainer callback ABC + handler (lifecycle hooks) with pluggable callbacks
- [ ] ✅ Built-in callbacks: checkpoint, evaluation, HF model save, HF Hub upload, ref-model update, DB registration
- [ ] ✅ Trackers: W&B and console logger (console needed where W&B init fails through HPC proxies); per-step commit toggle
- [ ] ✅ vLLM engine stats (throughput/KV/request) to console + tracker; optional Ray-Prometheus
- [ ] ✅ Resumable checkpointing: interval, resume-latest/from-path, max-to-keep, HF save interval, HF upload mode (latest/all)
- [ ] ✅ Eval cadence control (interval, eval-before-train, eval batch + n-samples, eval result dumps)
- [ ] ❌ In-the-loop full agentic-benchmark eval (terminal-bench / SWE-bench scored mid-training, distinct from held-out RL-reward eval)
- [ ] ✅ Reward-vs-steps / temporal / metrics-table exporters for run analysis
- [ ] ✅ Debug aids: data-batch dump, eval-results dump, GPU memory snapshots
- [ ] ❌ Unified DB/model-registry that always works offline (current Supabase registration assumes connectivity)

## Infra / ops
- [ ] ✅ SLURM multinode + Ray-cluster-in-container bring-up (head + attaching workers via RAY_ADDRESS)
- [ ] ✅ Multiple HPC clusters with per-cluster configs: **Leonardo** (A100-64, x86, CINECA), **Jupiter** (GH200, aarch64/cu13), **ALCC** (A100-80), **ZIH**, Perlmutter, Frontier (MI250x)
- [ ] ✅ Container runtimes: Apptainer/Singularity SIF + writable sandbox, baked-overlay vs bind-mount, podman; external uv venv from `uv.lock`
- [ ] ✅ Config-driven container env (sif / binds / pydeps / overlays / extra_env) reproducing hand-baked sbatch
- [ ] ✅ Daytona sandbox pooling: auto-snapshot caching, per-job concurrency cap, cross-cluster running-job cap
- [ ] ✅ Preemption recovery: resume-latest + frequent checkpointing + restart-chaining (interval=1 for multi-hour steps)
- [ ] ✅ Fully-offline operation on air-gapped compute nodes
- [ ] ⚠️ aarch64/cu13 (GH200) parity for the full stack (Megatron/TransformerEngine/DeepEP unproven there)
- [ ] ❌ Host-memory (CPU-RAM) pressure controls for high-concurrency + R3-capture rollouts (today mitigated by hand-cutting concurrency/worker counts)

---

### Honest gap flags
- **MoE + EP + grouped-GEMM + DeepEP + R3** are the least mature surface: ported and validated to a single 80B capstone training step, but **not production-hardened** for multi-step stability, and **DeepEP at scale + Megatron-path hybrid-arch support are missing**.
- **Router replay** is a framework-level patch everywhere (including megatron.core); a first-class, packing-and-EP-correct R3 is a true want.
- **SGLang, DeepSpeed, Megatron, LoRA, dynamic sampling, critic-based PPO** are implemented-but-unused — parity-on-paper, not exercised by us.
- **Auto-tuning** (memory-profiled microbatch/recompute, adaptive staleness controller, host-RAM pressure control) is entirely manual today.
</content>

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
🤖 ## Summary

Onboarding new users onto Iris is currently ad-hoc and high-friction, which is a drag on community engagement. This is a feature request for two complementary capabilities:

1. **More tiers of access on the Iris infra** — in particular a **sandboxed / limited-privilege user tier with lower scheduling priority**, so new or less-trusted community members can be granted constrained access without risk to production runs or the shared pools.
2. **A self-onboarding process for new users** — a form-driven flow where a prospective user signs any required releases/agreements and the necessary tracking info is captured automatically, so onboarding stops being a manual one-off.

The overall goal: make new-user onboarding into Iris **less ad-hoc and lower-friction**, to support broader community engagement while keeping the cluster safe.

## 1. Tiered access (sandboxed, limited-privilege, lower-priority)

Today access is effectively all-or-nothing. A constrained tier would let us say "yes" to community users quickly. Desired properties:

- **Lower scheduling priority** — sandboxed-tier jobs yield to production/interactive work (preempted first, scheduled last), so onboarding a new user can't starve real runs.
- **Limited privileges / resource caps** — per-user or per-tier quotas (max concurrent jobs, max TPU slice size/type, max wall-clock), and restricted access to sensitive buckets/secrets/clusters.
- **Isolation** — sandboxed users can't see or affect other users' jobs/data; ideally a constrained namespace.
- Tiers should be easy for an admin to assign/upgrade (e.g. promote a sandboxed user to standard once vetted).

(Implementation is up to the Iris owners — priority classes / scale-group limits / per-user quotas already exist in spirit; this asks for a first-class "sandboxed community" tier built on them.)

## 2. Self-onboarding flow

Replace the manual back-and-forth with a form a prospective user fills out that:

- Collects the identity/affiliation info the admin (Isaac) needs to **track** the user (name, affiliation, contact, intended use, sponsor/referrer).
- Has them **sign any required releases / usage agreements** as part of the flow.
- On submission, routes everything to Isaac (and/or provisions a sandboxed-tier account) so onboarding is one self-service step instead of ad-hoc DMs.

Net effect: a new community member can request access, sign what they need to sign, and land in the sandboxed tier with minimal admin toil.

## Why now
Community interest in Iris is growing; the current ad-hoc path doesn't scale and creates friction for both newcomers and admins. A constrained tier + self-onboarding form unblocks safe, low-effort community access.

---
*Filed on behalf of @benjaminfeuer. Assigning @Helw150 to triage / route to the Iris infra owners.*

issues.author: lukedhlee
issues.body:
**Scope: terminus-2 evals.**

**Summary.** In multi-turn terminus-2 evals, whether a model sees its own earlier thinking depends on the serving path, not on how the model was trained. Today (TITO off) Qwen sees the history its template was trained with; Snowball sees a format it was never trained on. With TITO on, both see exactly their sampled tokens, which matches Snowball's training and not Qwen's. This is not a bug in either setting. It is a protocol difference that the catalog does not record, and it sits inside every cross-model comparison.

**How each model was trained to see its history**

| model | earlier turns' thinking in the prompt |
|---|---|
| Snowball | kept, inline, with `<\|start_think\|>` / `<\|end_think\|>` markers, in every assistant turn (SFT and RL) |
| Qwen3 (and Nemotron, GLM) | dropped; only the earlier actions remain (terminus-2 sends observations as user turns; Qwen3's template keeps thinking only inside a tool-call cycle) |

## Status quo

**TITO off (current default)**

- *Qwen3 and peers:* no reasoning history. Matches training.
- *Snowball:* its earlier thinking is fed back, but as plain text with the markers stripped, and each observation opens with a parser warning ("extra text before the JSON object"). Neither its training format nor the peers' dropped format.

**TITO on**

- *Snowball:* full reasoning history with markers, byte-identical to training.
- *Qwen3 and peers:* full reasoning history, which their templates never showed them under terminus-2. It does match what they see when RL-trained on this stack, which always keeps thinking.

## What would make eval match each model's training template

| | Snowball (trained with thinking kept) | Qwen3 and peers (trained with thinking dropped) |
|---|---|---|
| TITO off | reasoning parser in the serving entry, so the thinking comes back as `reasoning_content` instead of leaking into the action, plus `interleaved_thinking: true` in the eval agent config, so harbor sends it back with each earlier turn (the Snowball template already renders it with the markers). The parser alone gives "dropped", like the peers. | already matches |
| TITO on | already matches | drop the think spans when building the next prompt (re-render the history without them). Eval only: the prompt is then no longer the exact served prefix, so this cannot be used for training on this stack. |

**What we measured (Snowball only).** 441 R2E-Gym tasks, same harness: dropping all prior thinking scored +.012 [−.005, +.028] over keeping; keeping only the last two spans +.017 [+.001, +.032]. Dropping made the model think less per turn and fit more actions in the budget. Nothing equivalent exists for Qwen.

Related: marin-community/harbor#124 (harbor's thinking/action split on the token path now recognises Snowball's markers).
issues.title: [eval] Evaluation history differs from training history for thinking models: what each model sees with TITO on vs off

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
## Problem

Marin's Harbor runner can safely re-run unscored trial directories after a managed inference interruption, but a fresh evaluation invocation has no way to request the same behavior.

This blocks coverage repair for a completed agentic evaluation. A Terminal-Bench 2.0 run produced 89 trial results, of which 82 had verifier results and seven were infrastructure-unscored. Re-invoking the same immutable policy preserves all 89 terminal results. Adding an infrastructure exception to `retry.include_exceptions` is not a valid workaround: Harbor correctly rejects that changed policy against the existing `lock.json`.

The runner already has the required safety boundary in `_remove_unscored_trials`: it removes a trial directory only when `verifier_result is None`, and preserves every scored result even if that result also carries an exception.

## Expected behavior

`HarborExecutor` should expose an explicit, default-off recovery option that applies the existing unscored-only prune immediately before a fresh Harbor resume. The option must:

- preserve the stable Harbor policy digest and job lock;
- preserve every result with a non-null `verifier_result`;
- remove only unscored or unreadable completed trial directories so Harbor re-plans them;
- remain disabled for ordinary runs;
- have regression coverage proving scored zero-reward outcomes are not removed.

## Evidence

The affected record is `20260911-000100-snowball-final-qk157-base-tb2-recovery-a432`: 89 attempted, 82 scored, with five `AgentSetupTimeoutError`, one tmux-loss `RuntimeError`, and one `AddTestsDirError`. A recovery invocation that changed `retry.include_exceptions` loaded the 89 results, then failed with:

```text
FileExistsError: Job directory ... already has a lock.json that does not match the resolved job lock.
```

No trial artifacts were changed by the rejected invocation.
issues.title: [eval] Allow explicit unscored Harbor recovery

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
## TL;DR

The [published analysis site](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/benjaminfeuer/nemotron-3-ultra-post-training-reconstruction/2026.09.11.1/index.html) reconstructs the Nemotron-3 Ultra post-training pipeline from the technical report and NVIDIA's public code, configurations, datasets, and model cards. It covers the cold start, all 15 specialist teachers in Figure 10, the RLVR self-teacher, both MOPD iterations, and runnable public proxies where released assets permit them. Each stage separates production evidence from reconstruction choices and includes pinned inputs, launch commands or explicit blockers, checkpoint gates, and compute estimates.

## Description

The Ultra report specifies the pipeline topology but omits many dataset snapshots, checkpoint identities, routing assignments, optimization settings, and second-round refresh procedures. The site maps each disclosed stage to the closest public NVIDIA implementation while retaining those unknowns.

The runnable safety proxy uses the Ultra-labeled indirect-prompt-injection release with its enterprise environments and deterministic trace verifier. AEGIS is recorded only as reviewed prior work and is not treated as Ultra training provenance.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Provide one evidence-backed reference that a researcher can use to inspect the reconstructed lineage, run the available public substitutes, and identify where production reproduction still depends on unreleased information.

## Status

The publication pass is complete. The site contains 15 specialist reports, one cold-start report, one self-teacher control report, and a cross-linked index. Static validation checked every report, pinned source, sample artifact, and runnable shell block. Browser smoke tests passed for navigation and filtering.

Two source-data gaps remain: PivotRL's replayable search-pivot pool, which is companion evidence rather than a disclosed Ultra production stage, and verifier-passing office responses for light office SFT. Several stages also need tested custom SFT packing configurations or unpublished training settings.

## Links

* Analysis site: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/benjaminfeuer/nemotron-3-ultra-post-training-reconstruction/2026.09.11.1/index.html
* Important updates: the follow-up comment lists the five highest-value missing artifacts or disclosures.

## Decision Log

* Treat the Ultra technical report as the authority for production lineage.
* Label later NVIDIA releases and companion methods as public proxies unless a source identifies them with Ultra training.
* Publish the reports as one versioned directory so all relative navigation and the bundled proxy-data materializer remain intact.

## Conclusion

The site provides an executable public reconstruction where NVIDIA has released the required data and stack. It does not claim bitwise or performance-level reproduction of the production pipeline.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
Marin's Harbor result reader currently marks a trial scoreable only when it has a verifier result and no exception. It then counts every exception type as attrition against the infrastructure-success gate.

That policy disagrees with Harbor's published `harbor-config` error contract. The contract classifies `AgentTimeoutError` and `ContextLengthExceededError` as agent-attributable outcomes, distinguishes infrastructure failures, and allows passthrough outcomes whose verifier result remains usable. Harbor runs the verifier after several benign agent outcomes, so a persisted exception does not by itself make a trial unscored.

Consume the error taxonomy from the exact `harbor-config` revision paired with the Harbor runtime. Use its categories to decide scoreability, infrastructure coverage, and resume behavior instead of maintaining an implicit `exception is None` policy in Marin.

Tracked by #8083. Harbor introduced the shared taxonomy in marin-community/harbor#57.

Done when:
- Infrastructure success counts only trials classified as infrastructure failures or otherwise ungraded by the shared contract.
- Agent-attributable outcomes such as `AgentTimeoutError` and `ContextLengthExceededError` remain valid trials and preserve the verifier result or contract-defined score treatment.
- Passthrough errors retain usable verifier scores.
- Unknown error names are surfaced as taxonomy drift instead of silently assigned a category.
- Eval records retain the per-type error histogram and the `harbor-config` revision used for classification.
- Tests cover infrastructure, agent, passthrough, unknown, and exception-free trials.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 Plan for this issue, implementation starting now.

The gap is a boundary, not a missing list. `harbor_config.errors` (marin-community/harbor#57) is installed only in the isolated Harbor environment, where Marin's own `trial_driver.py` runs. Trial classification happens later in the Marin process, in `runner.py::_read_trial`, which cannot import it. So `_read_trial` keeps a one-name set today.

The fix moves the taxonomy across that boundary as data, not code:

1. Preflight (`_preflight_one`) already returns a JSON payload to Marin. It will also return the `INFRASTRUCTURE`, `AGENT`, and `PASSTHROUGH` name lists from `errors_by_category`, plus the `harbor-config` package version. Because preflight and the job run in the same locked environment, the snapshot is from the exact revision that produced the trials.
2. `ValidatedHarborConfig` carries the snapshot into `HarborExecutor`, the same path #9105 used for agent context limits.
3. `_read_trial` classifies by lookup. Infrastructure: ungraded, counts against the 90% gate. Agent: graded with its reward. Passthrough: graded when a verifier result exists. A name in no list is unknown.
4. Unknown names are counted in the record's error histogram under their own key and fail admission, so a Harbor pin bump that adds an exception type is visible on the first run rather than absorbed.
5. `HarborRef` records the `harbor-config` version, so a reader knows which taxonomy classified a run. The per-type error histogram already exists and is unchanged.

Marin's process still never imports Harbor code. Tests cover infrastructure, agent, passthrough with and without a verifier result, unknown, and exception-free trials.

Tracked by #8083.

comments.body:
@penfever mentioned that the harbor-config error taxonomy is fairly lightweight as a dependency. He mentioned that they change often.

@penfever - is it sufficient to categorize errors according to the harbor version that ran it / the current harbor-config? Ie I'm assuming we're not looking for forwards compatibility?

<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This issue defines a 150-run learning-rate and token-budget sweep for the Aug/Hero MoE setup. It covers six model widths from d512 through d2048, five token budgets from 30x through 600x active parameters, and five LR multipliers around the May-Recipe MuonH recommendation. The goal is to see whether the recommended LR remains compute-optimal as both model size and training tokens scale, or whether the Aug/Hero recipe needs a systematic LR adjustment. Current status: the sweep is specified but no runs have been launched yet.

### Helpful links
- `experiments/grug/moe_hero_fsdp/sweep.md` on branch `aug_hero_run_ablations`
- #6711
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

Model sizes and architecture are fixed by the hero sweep table (`experiments/grug/moe_hero_fsdp/sweep.md`, branch `aug_hero_run_ablations`): d512, d768, d1024, d1280, d1536, d2048, each with its local/global KV split and explicit global-attention layers, a 1024-token sliding window, and sequence length 8192. The `60×` column in that table is the reference token budget; the other multipliers just scale the step count (batch is fixed per size).

## Goal

Map the compute-optimal learning rate relative to the May-Recipe heuristic across model size and token budget — i.e. whether the recommended LR holds, or needs a systematic multiplier, as we scale tokens (30×→600×) and width (d512→d2048).

## Sweep

- **Sizes (6):** d512, d768, d1024, d1280, d1536, d2048.
- **Token budgets (5):** 30×, 60×, 150×, 300×, 600× active params. 60× matches `sweep.md`; steps scale linearly.
- **LR multipliers (5):** 0.7, 0.85, 1.0, 1.2, 1.4 × the recommended MuonH LR.
- **Total: 6 × 5 × 5 = 150 runs.**

### Steps per (size × token budget)

| size | batch | 30× | 60× | 150× | 300× | 600× |
|------|------:|----:|----:|-----:|-----:|-----:|
| d512  |  32 | 2115 |  4230 | 10575 | 21150 |  42300 |
| d768  |  64 | 3172 |  6345 | 15862 | 31725 |  63450 |

| d1536 | 256 | 6238 | 12476 | 31191 | 62381 | 124762 |
| d2048 | 512 | 6221 | 12442 | 31106 | 62212 | 124425 |

### Recommended MuonH LR (1.0×) per (size × token budget)

The heuristic LR falls as tokens grow (`adam_lr ∝ tokens^-0.395`), so the base LR is per (size, token budget); each run multiplies its cell by {0.7, 0.85, 1.0, 1.2, 1.4}.

| size | 30× | 60× | 150× | 300× | 600× |

### Naming

`aug-hero-{size}-{mult}x-lr{lrmult}`, e.g. `aug-hero-d1024-150x-lr0.85`.

## Status

Defined; **no runs launched.**

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Aug hero LR sweep — results + LR scaling law.** Figures and analysis on branch [`grug-aug-lr-sweep-results`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/grug-aug-lr-sweep-results/experiments/grug/aug_lr_sweep_figs).

## Status: 122/150 cells at full budget

d512–d1536 mostly complete; the remaining ~28 are the largest/longest cells (d2048-300×/600×, d1536-600×), which crash-and-resume off temp checkpoints and are the long pole. Best paloma `macro_loss` per cell (metric used throughout):

| size | 30× | 60× | 150× | 300× | 600× |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| d512 | 3.844 | 3.666 | 3.502 | 3.409 | 3.336 |
| d768 | 3.467 | 3.325 | 3.185 | 3.104 | 3.048 |
| d1024 | 3.153 | 3.046 | 2.938 | 2.868 | 2.813 |
| d1280 | 2.994 | 2.899 | 2.802 | 2.740 | 2.692 |
| d1536 | 2.874 | 2.790 | 2.695 | 2.636 | (partial) |
| d2048 | 2.730 | 2.651 | (partial) | (partial) | (partial) |

## Per-cell LR optimum (log-quadratic fit)

Each cell's LR sweep fits a clean parabola in `log(LR)`; the optimum `lr*` **drifts up with token budget** — ~1.0× at 30× to **~1.2–1.4× at 300×/600×** — with a mild downward shift for wider models. The 1.0× heuristic is right for short runs but under-shoots the LR for over-trained budgets.

![per-cell](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/grug-aug-lr-sweep-results/experiments/grug/aug_lr_sweep_figs/lr_sweep_percell_fit_paloma.png?raw=true)

## Learned optimal-LR power law

Fitting the per-cell `lr*` (× the May-Recipe heuristic LR) to `lr = a·tokens^b·hidden^c·batch^0.5` (batch exponent pinned):

```
lr = 34.3 · tokens^-0.346 · hidden^-0.345 · batch^0.5      R² = 0.978, median rel err 1.6%
```

![powerlaw](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/grug-aug-lr-sweep-results/experiments/grug/aug_lr_sweep_figs/lr_powerlaw_fit.png?raw=true)

## Batch-controlled collapse

Dividing out `√batch` (and `hidden^c`) collapses **all 6 model sizes onto a single `tokens^-0.346` line**, R² = 0.979 — the optimal LR is a pure token power law once width and batch are controlled for.

![collapse](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/grug-aug-lr-sweep-results/experiments/grug/aug_lr_sweep_figs/lr_batch_collapse.png?raw=true)

## vs. current heuristic, and at the d6144 / 15T target

muonh LR = `coeff·tokens^p·hidden^q·batch^0.5` (seq 8192 folded into coeff):

| | coeff | tokens exp | hidden exp |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ours (fit)** | 34.35 | **−0.346** | **−0.345** |
| **current heuristic** | 25.89 | −0.395 | −0.150 |

Two structural disagreements: ours decays **slower with tokens** (wants more LR at large budgets) and **much faster with width**. At **d6144 / 15T tokens** these nearly cancel — our law prescribes **~1.07× the heuristic's LR** (batch-independent; e.g. batch 4096 → heuristic 2.80e-3 vs ours 2.99e-3).

**Caveat:** that agreement is a coincidental cancellation, and d6144/15T is a large extrapolation — width is **3× beyond** the widest swept model (d2048) and 15T is well past the 600× budget. The `hidden^-0.345` term (the biggest disagreement) is the least-constrained; a d6144-or-wider point is needed to pin it before trusting either law at 15T.

evaluation/task system with a frozen answer contract, a Qwen3-0.6B screening ladder, a MoE rung
(Qwen3-30B-A3B) used only where a dense model cannot answer, and Snowball confirmation with a
pre-registered non-inferiority margin. Weight-sync cost, the largest measured lever at Snowball
scale, is treated as engineering with bit-identical proofs, not as a research question.

## Description

The first epic (#8936) built the async trainer path, the telemetry, and the Grafana dashboard,
and produced controlled 25- and 100-update comparisons on Qwen3-0.6B and Snowball. It also found
that raw GSM8K reward hides nontermination (Snowball scored 120/128 raw with 64 completed
answers), that the cadence lever changes staleness and cost together, and that the drift
metric conflates engine mismatch with staleness. This epic starts from that evidence with a
narrative structure: goal → sub-goals → hypotheses → experiments, each experiment with a fixed
design bucket, a done-when, and a kill criterion.

Scope: non-agentic math; Megatron trainer; vLLM inference with existing flags only; H100.
Out of scope: agentic tasks, vLLM implementation work, GB200.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Snowball RL can run faster in wall-clock and GPU-hours at non-inferior held-out quality by
decoupling the trainer from rollout workers, and there is a measurable safe range of off-policy
age. A speedup is a hypothesis to test; the completion criterion is evidence with confidence
intervals and an operating recommendation.

Sub-goals: trustworthy measurement · a cost model of where training time goes · cheap weight
sync · off-policy tolerance · system balance (cadence, GPU split, admission) ·
learning-quality validity · trainer memory and speed · a scale ladder from Qwen3-0.6B to Snowball.

## How to read this thread

One comment per milestone or per experiment. Each comment has four parts: what we did and why,
results (with numbers and intervals), what this means, and what comes next. Provenance (commits,
receipts, W&B links, audit gates) is in a collapsed block at the end of each comment.

## Status

(one line per milestone, newest first)

- Milestone 1 — prior runs closed out: the isolated-TIS analysis and the canonical results table
  are posted; no configuration graduates on a single seed.
- Milestone 0 — program started: execution branches `atqamar/async-non-agentic-rl-v2` created
  from MarinSkyRL `fa6aae36` / Marin `eb85a25675`; preflight passed; answer contract frozen.

## Milestones

0 program started · 1 prior runs closed out · 2 evaluation and task system in place · 3
telemetry and pause fix landed · 4 answer contract and tasks fixed · 5 weight sync under 1.5 s
with bit-identical proof · 6 correction chosen and safe-bound rule · 7 learner-size decision · 8
system balance measured · 9 MoE-rung verdict · 10 final tradeoff statement with confidence intervals.

## Glossary

- **Cadence C** — sync weights to the rollout workers every C optimizer updates.
- **Age A** — the maximum number of updates a rollout group may lag the trainer and still be used.
- **P/I** — learner GPUs / inference GPUs.
- **Objectives** — behaviour-clip (BC), plain PPO (REG), PPO with truncated importance sampling
  (REG+TIS), and the masked/second-moment corrections to be added.
- **Three cost axes** — optimizer updates, consumed tokens, and GPU-hours plus core seconds.
- **Three quality scores** — the verifier's raw reward; the completed score (correct *and* the
  response ended on its own, not at the token cap), which is the ranking metric; and a semantic
  score (final answer checked after the thinking boundary).
- **Staleness** — policy-version lag in optimizer updates unless stated otherwise.

## Links

- Prior epic: #8936 (results that carry over are in the milestone-1 comments).
- Reference log this format follows: #8765.

## Decision Log

- 2026-09-08 — Eval battery replaces the locked 1,191-row GSM8K window with GSM8K-Platinum + MATH
  items (window at ceiling, some mislabeled items, informative signal collapses after 60
  updates); the old window stays as the legacy battery for closing the prior confirmation.
- 2026-09-08 — Weight-sync design: shard-to-shard NCCL send/recv (expert weights are already in
  vLLM's layout on the trainer under TP1/EP8); delta weight sync gated on density and on
  sync still mattering afterwards.
- 2026-09-08 — Non-inferiority margin: 2 pp on the completed score (default, revisable before the
  Snowball quality stage); seed count derived from the measured Snowball seed spread before
  confirmation launches.

🤖 Answer contract and prompt templates frozen for Qwen3-0.6B and Snowball

**What we did and why.** Every score in this program depends on the exact prompt template and
the rule the verifier applies to an answer. The first epic changed both mid-stream, which is
why its raw rewards were not comparable across runs. We recorded one template per model and
one contract per environment, hashed them, and added a test that fails if either changes.

with valid syntax, so the test bites.

fails at test time rather than silently producing incomparable numbers.

**What we did and why.** The first epic ran a six-arm Qwen3-0.6B screen (two sync
cadences × three objectives) but never analysed it. The question it can answer is whether the
truncated-importance-sampling correction (TIS) helps quality when rollouts are up to three
updates stale, which matters because letting rollouts go stale is how async training gets its
speed. We audited all six runs and compared the arms in pairs on the completed score (correct
*and* the response ended on its own), the ranking metric for this program. This is a historical
run: one training seed, the legacy GSM8K contract, and the small 128-question development set.

Paired contrasts on the completed score (98.75% paired percentile-bootstrap intervals, which
give simultaneous 95% coverage for the four comparisons; 100,000 draws; exact two-sided
McNemar p-values, Holm-adjusted):

| contrast | delta pp | simultaneous 95% interval | Holm-adjusted p |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| cadence 1: PPO+TIS − plain PPO | +75.00 | [+64.84, +84.38] | 1.0e-28 |
| cadence 1: behaviour-clip − plain PPO | +68.75 | [+58.59, +78.91] | 1.9e-26 |
| cadence 4: PPO+TIS − plain PPO | +7.81 | [−0.78, +17.19] | 0.105 |

[Quality versus updates, consumed tokens and core time; audited JSON and analysis source](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/artifacts/analysis/async-rl-v2-e0-audited-results/v0).

**What this means.**
1. At cadence 4 (the configuration that saves time), the TIS correction is worth +7.8 pp on
   completed answers with an interval that includes zero, and behaviour-clip is worth +6.3 pp,
   also including zero. On one seed this is not a resolved benefit.
2. At cadence 1, plain PPO's failure is almost entirely nontermination: it scored 94/128 on raw
   reward but only 2/128 completed, with 126/128 responses cut off at the token cap. Both
   corrections fix that (+75 and +69 pp, well outside the intervals). So the correction's
   clearest effect is on whether answers finish, not on whether they are right.
3. Fixed update counts are not equal work: consumed tokens range 5.4M–12.4M across arms, so the
   shorter core times at cadence 4 are not an equal-token speedup, and the group ages were not
   randomised. No configuration graduates from this analysis.

**Next.** Measure how much evaluation is needed to separate arms (the power calibration), then
run the staleness ladders on Qwen with two seeds and the new evaluation battery, where these
contrasts get real intervals. Milestone 1 (prior runs closed out) follows once the canonical
results table is posted.

<details><summary>Glossary and provenance</summary>

**Terms.** C = sync weights every C completed updates; A = maximum admitted rollout-group age in
updates (sync needs C ≤ A+1); realised age = trainer step minus the group's stamped
version at batch assembly, observed not randomised; behaviour-clip (BC) = objective with a
learner/behaviour ratio and its own clipping; plain PPO (REG) = no importance weighting; PPO+TIS
= truncated importance sampling with cap 2 on captured behaviour logprobs; completed score =
verifier-correct AND ended on its own, denominator all questions; semantic = independent
final-answer check, never inferred from raw reward; trunc % = fraction of responses ending at the
token cap; core seconds = rollout wait + learner + weight-sync loop time, excluding evaluation
and setup; task GPUh = allocated GPUs × actual task-running duration; ESS = effective sample
size of importance weights, minimum fraction over updates; dev = the reused 128-question
screening set, not held-out evidence.

**Sources.** Inherited rows are transcribed from the program's canonical table, each attributed
to the predecessor workstream's plan and/or the linked #8936 comment; the original audits called
each row fully audited (W&B, receipt, Finelog). The realised-age definition was verified in
MarinSkyRL `fully_async_trainer.py:1847–1856`. The six Qwen .16 runs: MarinSkyRL

🤖 Milestone 1: prior runs closed out; no configuration graduates on a single seed

**What we did and why.** Before new experiments, we finished what the first epic left open: the
unanalysed six-arm Qwen screen and a consolidated table of every audited run. Both are needed so
that the new program starts from what is actually known rather than from raw-reward rankings.

**Results.** The [TIS analysis](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8955#issuecomment-5582069530)
shows the corrections' clearest effect is on whether answers finish (+69 to +75 pp completed at
cadence 1) while their effect on quality at cadence 4 is +6 to +8 pp with intervals including
zero, on one seed. The [canonical results table](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8955#issuecomment-5582304402)
carries 14 inherited families plus seven newly audited runs, with the completed score shown next
to the raw reward and missing fields left explicit rather than imputed.

**What this means.** Every prior claim now has a place in one table with its provenance, and the
one open analysis is closed. Nothing graduates: the Qwen results are single-seed, and the Snowball
references vary by hundreds of completed answers across seeds.

**Next.** Milestone 2, the evaluation and task system: a versioned task pool with per-model
difficulty ratings, a dual scorer (verifier contract plus an independent semantic check), and a
seeded sampler, so that later comparisons have enough questions to separate arms. The seed-43
Snowball pair completes alongside.

🤖 Task pool built: nine parquet views with train/dev/held-out locks, verified by readback

**What we did and why.** Every experiment in this program samples its prompts from one
versioned pool rather than from whatever rows a recipe happened to slice, so that arms and
seeds compare on identical questions and held-out sets stay held out. This step built that pool:
each prompt carries a content hash, an answer type, the contract it is scored under, a licence
field, its split, and its token count under both models' templates, and the held-out rows are
locked in a manifest the sampler cannot cross.

**Results.** The pool artifact was written and read back: `KE1_ARTIFACT_READBACK_PASS`, all nine
parquet views and the split locks verified against the candidate manifest
`d39aa170289c9637427bb2f6a829b49321875aa1ebc054fbcda7150bd2482cc1`. Independent pool and sampler
tests: `21 passed in 20.19s`.

**What this means.** Prompt identity is now a hash, not a row index, so pairing across arms and
seeds is exact and reordering a file cannot silently break a comparison.

**Next.** The final evaluation battery and the remaining eval-system gates (scorer, harness,
difficulty ratings), towards milestone 2, "evaluation and task system in place".

comments.body:
🤖 Seeded sampler admits only audited prompts; removing that check fails three tests

**What we did and why.** Experiments request prompts through one function, `sample(pool, bins,
n, seed, model, split)`, which must be deterministic and must refuse two things: crossing a
split boundary, and returning a prompt whose statement or gold answer has not passed the pool
audit. Without the second refusal, a mislabeled question could enter a training or evaluation
set and quietly bias a comparison.

**Results.** `KE3_ACCEPT_ONLY_MUTATION_PASS`: with the audit-eligibility check removed, three
tests fail; with it restored the suite passes 21 tests, and an independent replay also passes 21.
Sampling now requires an accepted audit status bound to the immutable manifest and the verifier;
prompts whose audit entry is missing, pending, flagged, rejected, or belongs to another manifest
cannot enter a sample.

**What this means.** The sampler is proven to bite: the test that guards audit eligibility was
shown to fail when the guard is removed, which is the standard this program holds every gate to.

**Next.** The scorer and harness gates, then the difficulty-rating pass for both models, towards
milestone 2.

🤖 Syncing every 4 updates reduces Snowball core time by 29.3%, but three seeds do not establish equal answer quality

**What we did and why.** We completed the missing run in the legacy Snowball comparison and audited all three seed pairs. The question is whether syncing weights less often makes training faster while preserving completed answers, a prerequisite for recommending an asynchronous operating range. Both configurations trained for 100 updates with behaviour clipping: sync every 2 updates with maximum age 1, versus every 4 updates with maximum age 3. Evaluation used the same locked 1,191 GSM8K questions at the start and finish.

**Results.**

Completed score means the legacy binary verifier marked the answer correct and its stop label was accepted. Truncation means the generation hit its length cap. Semantic scoring is unavailable for these historical dumps.

| cadence and seed | updates | consumed tokens | core s | task H100h | completed score | semantic | trunc % | group age mean/p95 | min ESS fraction |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|---|---:|
| 2, seed 17 | 100 | 14,081,797 | 3759.33 | 59.3357 | 200/1191 | NA | 82.70 | 0.50/1 | 0.98897 |
| 2, seed 29 | 100 | 12,293,213 | 3594.76 | 57.6094 | 374/1191 | NA | 67.93 | 0.50/1 | 0.96900 |
| 2, seed 43 | 100 | 14,120,429 | 3768.46 | 58.5634 | 1024/1191 | NA | 7.89 | 0.50/1 | 0.48478 |
| 4, seed 17 | 100 | 18,793,379 | 2874.52 | 49.3480 | 510/1191 | NA | 56.00 | 1.50/3 | 0.98516 |
| 4, seed 29 | 100 | 15,837,574 | 2663.95 | 47.2133 | 6/1191 | NA | 99.41 | 1.50/3 | 0.94917 |
| 4, seed 43 | 100 | 12,043,386 | 2323.28 | 42.4302 | 1056/1191 | NA | 6.88 | 1.50/3 | 0.97464 |

The completed-score differences for cadence 4 minus cadence 2 are **+26.03, −30.90, and +2.69 percentage points**, averaging **−0.73 pp**.

| uncertainty calculation | 95% interval for the mean completed-score difference |
|---|---|
| Paired questions, conditional on these three fixed training seeds | [−2.27, +0.81] pp |
| Paired training-seed effects, fixed question battery, Student-t with 2 degrees of freedom | [−71.82, +70.36] pp |

The question interval uses 10,000 paired bootstrap draws and does not measure uncertainty over new training seeds. The seed interval assumes approximately normal seed effects, which cannot be checked with three seeds; its width exposes how little these runs establish about reproducibility. Both lower bounds fall below the approved −2 pp non-inferiority margin.

Across the three seeds, cadence 4 uses **7,861.75 versus 11,122.55 core seconds** (29.3% less), **138.99 versus 175.51 task H100-hours** (20.8% less), and **46.67 versus 40.50 million consumed response tokens** (15.3% more). These are fixed-update comparisons, not equal-token speedups. The six-run cost is **314.50 H100-hours**, of which **42.43** is the newly executed candidate; the other five runs are inherited.

[Quality versus updates, consumed tokens and core time; audited summary and source](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/artifacts/analysis/async-rl-v2-e02-audited-results/v0).

**What this means.** The slower weight-sync schedule saves measured training time, but answer completion changes direction across seeds, so equal quality is **undecided** and no configuration graduates. Raw verifier reward hides the failure: the cadence-4 seed-29 run has 1,080 raw-correct answers but only 6 completed-correct answers, with 1,184 responses truncated. Sync cadence and permitted age changed together, actual consumed training order was not verified, and these historical runs cannot identify a causal age threshold.

**Next.** Finish the evaluation and task system, calibrate its power, and address nontermination before ranking new schedules. The next milestone is **evaluation and task system in place**; subsequent confirmation will use a frozen protocol and enough training seeds to support the quality decision.

🤖 Weight sync takes a median 20.226 seconds; receiver GPU telemetry is incomplete

**What we did and why.** We measured where Snowball spends time syncing updated weights to its rollout workers, to guide faster training at the same answer quality (E3.0). The run kept the existing five-second pause grace and tensor-by-tensor transfer behavior, using 32 learner and eight inference H100s for five updates. A 128-row training slice with zero data-loader workers exercised an epoch reset, while greedy evaluation ran on the same 128 development rows before training and after update five.

**Results.** [Audited JSON, three vector plots, and reproducible inputs](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/artifacts/analysis/async-rl-v2-weight-sync-baseline/v0) accompany the tables below.

All five updates, both evaluation dumps, and all five GPU tasks completed successfully. The run consumed 698,807 response tokens in 281.748 core seconds and cost 9.522493333 task H100-hours, including startup and evaluation.

| Whole-operation wall time | Median seconds | p95 seconds |
|---|---:|---:|
| Pause generation | 5.151 | 5.502 |
| Weight broadcast | 14.955 | 15.176 |
| Complete weight sync | 20.226 | 20.513 |
| Derived trainer stall | 20.154 | 20.434 |

Each row contains the five post-update syncs; startup is retained in the audit but excluded from these summaries. The stall proxy is the existing whole-sync wall time minus the host-side NCCL-send span; it is not GPU idle time. These are descriptive within-run quantiles, without a paired effect estimate or a confidence interval for a speedup.

| Stage | Wall median / p95, seconds | CUDA-event median / p95, milliseconds | Observation grouping |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Export | 5.569 / 6.937 | 5,738.414 / 7,067.907 | Maximum across 32 learner ranks per sync |
| NCCL send | 0.074 / 0.081 | 2,838.650 / 2,841.202 | Learner rank zero per sync |
| RPC wait | 5.367 / 5.458 | 2,612.828 / 2,688.714 | Learner rank zero per sync |
| Barrier | 6.187 / 6.454 | 6,045.054 / 6,324.449 | Maximum across 32 learner ranks per sync |
| Learner reload finalization | 0.00647 / 0.00686 | 6.493 / 6.890 | Learner rank zero per sync |
| Receive | 0.0602 / 0.0618 | Missing | Maximum receiver wall time per sync |
| Load | 4.544 / 4.630 | Missing | Maximum receiver wall time per sync |
| Receiver finalization | 0.00473 / 0.00490 | Missing | Maximum receiver wall time per sync |

All stage summaries contain five syncs. Export and barrier each have 160 underlying learner-rank observations; the other learner stages each have five. Including startup, 402 native learner stage events were retained. All 25 post-update learner wall maxima match the corresponding W&B driver metrics. Receiver wall maxima are retained in W&B, but individual receiver receipts and their CUDA times were not durably exported. The worker process returns those values over RPC without initializing a telemetry exporter.

Stage spans overlap. CUDA events can include stream waiting, while a host NCCL call can return before transfer completion; neither rank maxima nor stage medians may be summed into critical-path latency or GPU utilization.

The one-second inference polling configuration produced 2,648 cumulative token observations across eight engines. Actual sampling intervals reached 3.521 seconds. Counter differences aligned to each sync are retained with 60-second windows on either side; adjacent windows overlap other syncs and evaluation, so they do not establish a causal throughput effect. The final after-window has only 66.585% coverage and has no reported rate.

| Development evaluation | Contract score, 95% interval | Completed contract score, 95% interval | Length-stop fraction, 95% interval |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Before training | 75.00% [66.84, 81.70] | 73.44% [65.18, 80.32] | 11.72% [7.23, 18.44] |
| After five updates | 92.19% [86.22, 95.70] | 89.06% [82.48, 93.37] | 9.38% [5.44, 15.67] |

Intervals are Wilson intervals over 128 audited rows, not seed uncertainty or a paired treatment comparison. These are the retained legacy verifier and completed-stop scores; independent semantic scoring was not part of this timing gate. All 160 consumed groups have native policy-version age observations: 92 at age zero and 68 at age one. Pooled group-weighted mean age is 0.425 updates and nearest-rank p95 is one update; coverage is 32 groups per update. Behavior-ratio token-weight ESS fraction ranged from 0.991226 to 0.992424.

The separate data-loader gate failed its strict maximum-lag requirement: 373 samples included three values above two seconds, with a maximum of 2.527699 seconds. The three violations overlap weight sync; overlap does not establish their cause. The epoch reset was observed at update five, and evaluation at both required steps was verified. No lag sample reached ten seconds, but that does not satisfy the two-second criterion.

The preliminary Qwen two-GPU tests passed stage readback and the native pause precursor. Across 64 actual in-flight requests, the precursor accounted for 64 aborts and eventual completions, with zero lost requests and native first-token timestamps on every abort response. Those two tests cost 0.278617778 task H100-hours combined. They are engineering checks, not a Snowball speedup or the full repeated-sync pause gate.

**What this means.** The fixed pause and coordination spans are material optimization targets, and the whole-sync wall baseline is usable. The complete GPU-stage observability requirement remains unmet because receiver CUDA receipts were not retained. The loader change remains ungated; this five-update timing run establishes neither a quality improvement nor a recommended off-policy age range.

**Next.** Preserve receiver timing origin while exporting the native RPC receipts through the trainer, then validate the repair before a bounded Snowball rerun. Independently complete the pause-handshake checks with a matched stale-token comparison, and investigate the three lag spikes without excluding them or relaxing the threshold. These steps lead toward the telemetry and pause-fix milestone.

🤖 **Five Snowball updates stay below the event-loop lag limit**

**What we did and why.** We reran the five-update Snowball gate after the CPU profile identified
repeated tokenizer serialization as the remaining event-loop stall. The runtime changes only
omit the tokenizer from remote weight-sync client copies and repair receiver stage export.
The baseline zero-worker loader, original five-second pause grace and admission rules remain.
This is a timing mechanism test using the inherited binary GSM8K contract, not a quality-ranked
experiment. P32/I8, bf16, seed 17, C1/A1, train/dev 128/128, G4, context 8,192 and output cap
4,096 are identical to the failed trace. Eval runs at 0/5 and the fifth update crosses an epoch.

**Results.** All five updates finished, with the expected epoch reset on update five and eval at steps zero and five. Maximum event-loop lag was **1.116 seconds**, below the strict two-second limit.
All final task-window samples are retained, including 59 at step 0, 67 at step 4 and 86 at
step 5. The previous strict maximum was 2.527699240 seconds. The repaired trace contains all
546 stage events across six weight syncs, including 144 receiver events from eight distinct
origin ranks; 40 native stage max folds match W&B row by row.
Whole weight-sync p50/p95 was **17.010/17.480 seconds**, compared with 20.226/20.513 seconds in the original trace. The pause remains five seconds (repaired p50 5.235 seconds). This is a descriptive comparison of two runs; overlapping stage clocks are not additive.
The five successful east H100 task attempts cost **9.22088 task GPUh**; zero failures or
preemptions. Native terminal/runtime/request/attempt and all 256 eval rows were audited.

Eval wall times were 43.716/41.272 seconds at 0/5 versus 42.398/40.228 seconds in the failed
trace, increases of 3.11%/2.60%; total core time fell from 281.748 to 259.819 seconds. These
single-run timings do not establish a formal equivalence interval. Quality is also not
established: final completed-stop correctness fell from 114/128 to 104/128, a paired-prompt
conditional difference of −7.8125 pp (95% bootstrap interval −14.84375 to −0.78125 pp;
6 wins, 16 losses). Startup completed scores were 94/128 versus 93/128, difference −0.78125 pp
(interval −3.90625 to 2.34375). Final raw scores were 118/128 versus 108/128; truncations rose
from 12/128 to 20/128. Semantic scoring was not run. The comparison conditions on these two
realized runs and does not estimate seed variability or satisfy confirmation/non-inferiority.

**What this means.** The strict Snowball lag and receiver-observability mechanisms pass.
Together with the previously audited matched Qwen loader gate, this qualifies the loader and weight-sync telemetry repairs. It does not show quality preservation. The async consumed-order control is
still the next required gate before interpreting quality differences between these traces.
The weight-sync repair keeps the tokenizer on the driver and changes no optimizer operation.

**Next.** Complete the consumed-order and pooled-ratio qualification gates before interpreting quality differences. Run the matched Qwen pause-handshake comparison with the same serialization and telemetry repairs in both arms.

🤖 **A 20-update baseline fails the gate after an engine dies during startup**

**What we did and why.** We ran the original five-second-pause Qwen baseline for a matched comparison of weight-sync handshakes. The comparison requires clean operation throughout startup and training. An inference engine died during initialization, so we held the candidate and let the baseline finish to preserve its evidence.

**Results.** The baseline completed 20 updates and both evaluation dumps. Its two GPU tasks succeeded once, with no Iris retries or preemptions, costing **2.43432 task H100-hours**. Core training took 249.105 seconds and consumed 833,483 response tokens and the same number of loss tokens across 5,120 responses. Median pause was 5.027 seconds. Group-weighted mean age was 0.9 updates and pooled group p95 was 1; the consume-time token-weight ESS fraction ranged from 0.996439 to 0.998892.

The native ledger contains 1,344 completed training groups and 877,470 generated tokens, including 64 groups discarded at the epoch boundary. No completed tokens were rejected for staleness. Generated and consumed tokens have different denominators.

Initial and final completed correctness were 9/128 and 80/128, equal to raw correctness at both endpoints. Length stops increased from 1/128 to 4/128. The within-run paired-prompt improvement was 55.46875 percentage points, with conditional 95% bootstrap interval [46.875, 64.0625], 71 wins and no losses. Semantic scores were not computed.

During startup, an EngineCore failed to bind its TCPStore port with `EADDRINUSE`. The runtime retried initialization internally. That engine death **fails the whole-job gate**, despite the clean terminal training receipts. The candidate was never submitted for this pair.

**What this means.** Iris task success does not establish an error-free engine lifetime. The baseline measures the original pause but cannot qualify the matched handshake comparison. Its development-score change provides no quality-preservation or non-inferiority conclusion.

**Next.** Audit the refreshed pair, which has now finished with independent engines initialized sequentially in both arms. Its candidate has incomplete request-accounting receipts, so those require repair and a new qualification before accepting a pause reduction. These checks lead to the telemetry and pause-fix milestone.

🤖 Qwen rates 1,024 questions, then the larger run exposes a renderer mismatch

**What we did and why.**

We tested inference-only difficulty ratings to choose tasks for faster Snowball training at the same answer quality. A 16-question functional check preceded a 1,024-question pilot sampled proportionally across eight accepted training bins, with eight responses per question. Independent CPU audits checked original engine tokens, native rewards and completed correctness; the serving path also required exact agreement between API text and token decoding. We then attempted the 13,407-question remainder and a bounded 512-question diagnostic after the remainder failed that check.

**Results.**

| Attempt | Planned questions×responses | Audited rating rows | Audited response tokens | Native task seconds | H100-hours | Outcome |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Functional check | 16×8 | 128 | 36,033 | 158.510 | 0.044031 | Token/reward/completion parity passed |
| Representative pilot | 1,024×8 | 8,192 | 2,068,195 | 242.926 | 0.067479 | Token/reward/completion parity passed |
| Remainder | 13,407×8 | — | — | 234.651 | 0.065181 | Renderer mismatch; no rating dump |
| Diagnostic | 512×8 | — | — | 156.638 | 0.043511 | Same check failed; offending response captured |

All four attempts used one east H100, with no automatic retries. Total measured cost is 0.220201389 H100-hours. These were inference-only jobs: training updates, off-policy age and ESS do not apply; no training-core speedup is claimed. The pilot's generation plus native scoring took 129.002900501s within its 242.926s task allocation; the functional check predates that timing instrumentation.

Pilot completed correctness was 1,909/8,192=23.30%, with a 95% question-bootstrap interval [22.19%,24.48%]. The functional prerequisite checked 256 original token hashes; the pilot checked 16,384. The functional panel was deliberately small and balanced across bins, so its answer scores are not pooled with the representative pilot.

| Pilot bin | Questions | Completed correctness%,95% interval | Length stops/responses | Mean response tokens |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Procedural sums, easy | 43 | 90.41 [86.34, 93.90] | 0/344 | 28.8 |
| Procedural sums, medium | 68 | 81.43 [77.94, 84.93] | 0/544 | 70.5 |
| Procedural sums, hard | 68 | 32.17 [27.21, 37.32] | 0/544 | 174.5 |
| GSM8K | 423 | 8.89 [7.71, 10.14] | 1/3384 | 155.2 |
| MATH levels 1–2 | 108 | 32.52 [27.43, 37.73] | 1/864 | 241.4 |
| MATH level 3 | 89 | 24.72 [19.38, 30.34] | 0/712 | 336.9 |
| MATH level 4 | 95 | 18.29 [14.08, 22.76] | 4/760 | 459.5 |
| MATH level 5 | 130 | 7.98 [5.38, 10.96] | 11/1040 | 579.0 |

Completed correctness is full native credit multiplied by an accepted stop. Each question contributes the mean of its eight binary outcomes. Intervals resample questions with all eight responses kept together, 10,000 draws, bootstrap seed 17; the pooled interval preserves the pilot's bin quotas. They are descriptive, pointwise intervals conditional on one engine seed, with no simultaneous-coverage, independent-seed or treatment-comparison claim. The eight-sample per-question ratings remain coarse empirical measurements, not known latent probabilities.

The pilot had 8,175 accepted stops and 17 length stops (0.2075%); all length-stopped responses had completed correctness 0. All 8,192 thinking-boundary fields were populated. Its signed/fractional raw reward mean was −0.086208839; raw values were preserved separately from binary correctness. Semantic scoring returned numeric values for 7,924 rows and left 268 unresolved (236 ambiguous, 17 conflicting, 15 unparseable). One unlocalized Math-Verify comparison-timeout warning remains recorded; numeric return values do not certify that every underlying comparison completed.

The diagnostic preserved a 67,207-byte response artifact. In one procedural-sum response, generation stopped at 2,048 tokens inside a UTF-8 character: whole-sequence decoding emitted an extra replacement character. Replaying the exact pinned engine's incremental decoder matched the original API text for all eight responses, including the failing one; the other seven also matched whole-sequence decoding. The failed check remained strict, and neither failed attempt produced an accepted rating dump.

**What this means.**

The pilot is retained as an audited functional, cost and difficulty measurement. The full rating stage is held: a real rendering edge escaped the smaller probes, and the captured response now supplies a regression case. The correction must reproduce the engine's incremental decoding while preserving original tokens, forensic text and semantic scoring; it has not yet passed its repair gate. The initial whole-pool throughput projection is not a completed-run measurement, and these runs support no training-quality ranking or Snowball result.

**Next.**

Qualify the incremental renderer against the captured failure, EOS/stop and Unicode controls, and all 8,192 original pilot responses. Then review a fresh complete Qwen rating request on the corrected source within the remaining five-H100-hour rating budget. Snowball's native rating precursor remains held until the correction is qualified; the next milestone is the completed evaluation and task system.

🤖 3 seeded controls time out before their first recorded evaluation

**What we did and why.**

We ran a seeded control to test whether synchronous training and asynchronous training with no admitted staleness consume comparable work. This matters for attributing faster Snowball training at the same answer quality to scheduling. An earlier comparison consumed matching question sets but exceeded its prescribed reward-noise band, so the planned follow-up assigned each trajectory a seed derived from its question, sample and installed weight version and enabled the pinned engine's batch-invariance mode. The three arms were synchronous seed 17, asynchronous seed 17 and an asynchronous seed-29 noise reference, each planned for eight updates.

**Results.**

| Arm | Planned updates | Recorded training/evaluation result | Native terminal state | Task H100-hours |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| Synchronous, seed 17 | 8 | No usable result | Both tasks timed out | Unavailable |
| Asynchronous, seed 17 | 8 | No usable result | Both tasks timed out | Unavailable |
| Asynchronous noise reference, seed 29 | 8 | No usable result | Both tasks timed out | Unavailable |

All six GPU tasks failed on their first attempt, with no preemption or automatic retry. Each arm requested 16 east H100s with a 1,125-second execution timeout. The controller reports execution timeout for every task, but their attempt-finish timestamps are missing. The 15-H100-hour reservation therefore remains held; it is not reported as measured cost, and the job-terminal timestamps are not substituted for allocation ends.

All three W&B runs are marked crashed with zero history rows. Independent regional storage reads found no evaluation exports, successful training receipts or terminal manifests at the exact frozen output paths. Native telemetry contains no recorded optimizer updates, training metrics or completed-work events for these runs. Consumed tokens, training-core time, completed correctness, semantic correctness, truncation, age, ESS and confidence intervals are consequently unavailable.

The runs reached receiver setup and then stopped making visible progress before initial evaluation. Source inspection shows that batch-invariance initialization changes NCCL settings in the rollout workers while the trainer retains its previous settings. That is a transport hypothesis, not a demonstrated cause: the captured stacks cover the waiting launcher, and targeted computational stacks could not be recovered before teardown. The earlier two-request determinism probe passed, but it did not exercise trainer-to-worker weight sync.

**What this means.**

This attempt does not establish synchronous/asynchronous equivalence or non-equivalence. It is a failed startup qualification with no quality comparison. The earlier reward-noise failure remains unresolved, and the seeded implementation stays isolated from the shared branch.

**Next.**

Test the exact pinned transport initialization with two GPUs and three bounded cases: original settings, receiver-only batch-invariance settings, and matching settings on both sides. Review the measured outcome before any further training attempt. The next milestone remains telemetry and the pause fix landed.

🤖 2 Snowball startup probes stop before rating any answers

**What we did and why.** We attempted a small inference-only qualification before rating Snowball's training pool. Both requests used the same 16 questions, four responses per question, original east-region BF16 weights and frozen sampling protocol. The intended result was a verified model load and 64 audited responses, allowing task selection for faster Snowball training at the same answer quality.

**Results.** Neither attempt generated an answer.

| Attempt | Physical H100s | Initiating failure | Task H100 hours |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| Tensor parallelism 8 | 8 | Model configuration rejects 20 attention heads split across eight ranks | 0.133373333333 |
| Tensor parallelism 1, data/expert parallelism 4 | 4 | Container OOM kill during model loading | 0.080462222222 |

The first CPU preparation checked architecture and context limits but missed the pinned model's parallelism restrictions. Subsequent source and native configuration checks established that its GPU implementation requires tensor parallelism one; expert parallelism provides the supported weight sharding. The second attempt reached all four intended expert ranks, each assigned 64 of the model's 256 experts, then was OOM-killed while loading. The task exited 137 after 72.416 seconds at a 128 GiB host-memory limit. No CUDA out-of-memory traceback was recorded, and peak host memory was not available in the retained task receipt.

The loader source exposes a concrete capacity mismatch: each worker defaults to a 40,000,000,000-byte CPU buffer. Four such buffers total 160 GB, exceeding the container's 137,438,953,472-byte limit before other memory use. Each worker streams the checkpoint tensors to CPU and clones them before model-specific expert selection; expert parallelism does not prevent those overlapping host allocations. This is source-backed capacity analysis, not a measurement of the failed run's peak memory.

Both attempts used one task, with no retries or preemptions. No model-load, GPU-headroom or response-rendering gate passed. Quality, tokens, core training throughput, age, ESS, truncation and confidence intervals are unavailable because no inference or learning completed.

**What this means.** The initial layout was incompatible with the pinned model. The corrected layout progressed further, but its loader memory was not bounded for four workers. The second failure does not establish that the model cannot fit on four GPUs.

**Next.** Keep the model, BF16 precision, expert layout and sampling fixed. Review an explicit 8 GiB buffer limit and concurrency four per worker, plus periodic container-memory evidence, before another bounded load probe. Require successful loading and all 64 response audits before expanding the rating job. The next related milestone is the eval and task system in place.

**What we did and why.** Repeated the one-engine Qwen3-0.6B queue measurement with the concurrency cap reduced from eight to four. The task failed with exit 1, one attempt and no retry, after 227.815 seconds, costing 0.063281944444 H100 hours against the 0.166666666667-hour ceiling. The failure occurred in the identity ledger's strict subset check at the pause boundary.

The first read spanned 4.947766–4.951584 seconds after all admissions: 56 requests were unfinished, including 52 without a first token. The second read spanned 13.137458–13.141367 seconds: 40 were unfinished, including 36 without a first token. The separate pre-grace read still saw those 40. No successful native pause was recorded. Failure cleanup returned 36 logical results and canceled 28 logical tasks; each returned result contained 1,024 tokens and finite log probabilities, totaling 36,864 completed logical tokens. Cancellation is not eventual completion.

All 36 receipt chunks were retained and independently reassembled. Through the last pre-grace snapshot, the native ledger accounts for 64 starts, 24 length terminals containing 24,576 tokens and 40 active identities. It has no post-failure native drain. Consequently, neither full emitted-token conservation nor terminal resolution of all native requests can be established from this failed run. The measured protocol lasted 18.431902 seconds. This fixture had zero learner updates and no consumed training tokens, scorer or evaluation: training throughput, off-policy age, ESS, raw/contract-completed correctness and confidence intervals are not applicable. All 36 returned outputs intentionally reached the length limit; the other 28 logical tasks were canceled.
